items.title: Your body can make antibodies against molecules that don't exist yet
items.claim: Humans have about 20,000 genes. We make perhaps 10 to the 11 different antibody molecules — far more than our genome could encode directly. Including antibodies against viruses we'll never meet.
items.prompt: How do we generate such enormous antibody diversity?

options.text: Each antibody is encoded by a separate gene

V(D)J recombination — during B cell development, gene segments (V, D, J) are randomly chosen and joined with imprecise cuts, and then somatic hypermutation refines the result during an immune response
Antibodies are made up new for each encounter from scratch
The genome reshuffles itself constantly in all cells

items.reveal_title: Tonegawa's discovery — recombination in somatic cells
items.reveal:
Susumu Tonegawa (Nobel 1987) showed that B cells deliberately rearrange their immunoglobulin genes. Each B cell randomly picks one V, one D and one J segment for the heavy chain (V and J for the light chain), joins them with imprecise junctions (adding/deleting nucleotides), and pairs heavy with light. The combinatorial maths gives about 10 to the 11 possible specificities from a few hundred gene segments.

Once a B cell encounters its antigen, somatic hypermutation introduces additional point mutations into the variable region, and selection retains the best binders (affinity maturation).

The result is an immune system that can respond to virtually any molecular shape — including ones never seen before, like artificial drugs.
items.why: Genome size limits direct encoding. The immune system uses combinatorics and somatic mutation to overshoot what the genome alone could specify.

items.title: Bees die when they sting — and this makes evolutionary sense
items.claim: A worker bee that stings a mammal disembowels itself and dies. Sterile, suicidal workers shouldn't exist if natural selection works at the individual level. They do exist, abundantly.
items.prompt: How does evolution favour individuals that don't reproduce?

options.text: Natural selection doesn't really work for social insects

Hamilton's rule: a gene for altruism spreads if rB is greater than C (relatedness times benefit exceeds cost); worker bees share 75 percent of their genes with sisters due to haplodiploidy, so helping the queen reproduce passes on their own genes effectively
Queen bees control workers chemically against their interests

items.reveal:
W. D. Hamilton wrote the equation rB greater than C: a gene for helping behaviour spreads if the relatedness (r) times the benefit to the recipient (B) exceeds the cost to the actor (C).

In haplodiploid Hymenoptera (bees, ants, wasps), females are diploid (from a diploid mother and a haploid father), males are haploid (unfertilised eggs). A worker shares 50 percent of her genes with her own offspring (if she had any), but 75 percent with her full sisters — because their shared father is haploid and gave them ALL his genes.

So a worker's gene-propagation interest is best served by helping her mother (the queen) make more sisters. Sterility is rational from the gene's perspective.

Hamilton's work, building on J. B. S. Haldane's quip 'I would lay down my life for two brothers or eight cousins', founded sociobiology.
items.why: Selection is taught as acting on individuals. The gene's-eye view explains altruism, sociality and self-sacrifice — phenomena that the individual-level view can't easily handle.

items.title: Your mitochondria used to be a separate organism
items.claim: Mitochondria have their own DNA, their own ribosomes, a double membrane, and divide independently of the cell. About 2 billion years ago, a free-living alpha-proteobacterium got engulfed by another cell and stayed.
items.prompt: What's the strongest evidence mitochondria were once independent?

options.text: They are smaller than the host cell

Mitochondrial DNA is circular (like a bacterial chromosome), their ribosomes resemble bacterial ribosomes (and are inhibited by antibiotics like chloramphenicol), and their inner membrane has bacteria-like lipid composition

items.reveal_title: Lynn Margulis and the endosymbiotic theory
items.reveal:
Lynn Margulis proposed in 1967 that mitochondria descend from free-living alpha-proteobacteria, and chloroplasts from cyanobacteria. Her paper was rejected fifteen times before being accepted. The orthodoxy disliked the idea of major evolution happening by merger rather than gradual modification.

The evidence accumulated:
- Circular DNA in mitochondria and chloroplasts.
- Bacterial-style ribosomes; sensitive to bacterial antibiotics.
- Double membranes (the outer from the host cell, the inner from the bacterium).
- Replication by binary fission, independent of cell division.
- Phylogenetic analysis: mitochondrial genes group with Rickettsia (intracellular alpha-proteobacteria).

All eukaryotes (including animals, plants, fungi) descend from this single ancient merger. Without it, complex life wouldn't exist.
items.why: Evolution is taught as branching divergence. Some of the most important steps came from merger — two organisms becoming one.
